To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
larger diatoms allocate more of their cellular nitrogen to RBCS to counter slower RBC turnover rates.

Larger marine centric diatom species allocate more cellular nitrogen (by 3 fold) to the RUBISCO carbon assimilation complex than do smaller diatoms, to compensate for the slower turnover rate of the RUBISCO complex in the larger cells.
larger diatoms allocate more of their cellular nitrogen to photosynthetic protein complexes to compensate for their slower RUBISCO protein turnover rates.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the metabolic costs of photosynthesis, and the allocation of cellular resources to photosynthesis, across the cell size range of marine phytoplankton, and the implications of this for their growth and productivity under changing pCO2.
the physiological and molecular mechanisms that enable large and small diatoms to maintain similar photosynthetic carbon assimilation rates
the cellular nitrogen resource allocations of diatoms, the largest phytoplankton in the world’s oceans.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
large centric diatoms have a higher allocation of their cellular nitrogen to photosynthetic proteins, and this is particularly the case for RUBISCO.
large centric diatoms have a higher cellular nitrogen cost to photosynthesis, which may have implications for their growth under nitrogen limited conditions.
large centric diatoms have evolved to allocate a higher proportion of their cellular nitrogen to the RUBISCO carbon assimilation complex to offset slower turnover rates of RUBISCO.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

large diatoms allocate a greater fraction of their cellular nitrogen to photosynthetic protein complexes than do small diatoms, but this is counterbalanced by slower turnover rates of the key protein complexes in large diatoms.
the larger the diatom cell, the more cellular nitrogen it allocates to photosynthesis, and the lower its achieved photosynthetic rate per RUBISCO large-subunit.
larger centric diatoms have a lower turnover of their photosynthetic machinery, which they counter with a higher allocation of nitrogen to RUBISC.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the photosynthetic nitrogen cost per carbon assimilated increases with cell size.
the higher nitrogen costs for RUBISCO in large diatoms are offset by their greater light harvesting capacity, and that these trade-offs are not influenced by future pCO2.

the higher allocation of cellular N to RUBISCO and lower RUBISCO turnover in larger cells are key features of diatom physiology, enabling them to maintain comparable rates of photosynthetic carbon assimilation across a wide range of cell sizes.
